intro: This stretch of the Mon River, right at the edge of Washington County near Clairton, grew up around steel and power generation more than farmland, and that shows in the deed history. A lot of Elrama-area properties were developed for industrial or residential use with little regard for what was underground, while other, larger tracts further from the river retained the more typical farmland mineral history common elsewhere in the county.
If you own property near Elrama and aren't sure whether mineral rights come with it, we're glad to check the recorded deed and tell you plainly what we find.

sections.heading: Industrial River Corridor, Mixed Deed History
paragraphs: Because this part of the Mon Valley developed around industry rather than agriculture, mineral ownership near Elrama is genuinely inconsistent from parcel to parcel. Some properties never had minerals severed at all. Others, particularly larger tracts further from the immediate river corridor, followed the more typical pattern of coal severance followed by later gas leasing. We check your specific deed rather than assuming based on the general area.
This inconsistency is exactly why we do title research before ever discussing a number with an Elrama-area owner.
